Read it top to bottom, or jump around: every section starts with one line. The grey boxes marked Try it are live, so move the sliders. Nothing here assumes you already know reinforcement learning.

1. The whole idea

In one line. A neural network looks at what one automated vehicle knows, picks a target headway for it, and is nudged after each batch of driving so that choices which went better than expected become more likely. Nothing else is learned: no road model, no physics, no rule.

Section 8 runs this loop live on one real vehicle, and section 6 opens the agent box neuron by neuron.

16 → 4numbers in → probabilities out
5,508numbers in the policy
1 knobtau, the target headway. Not speed, not lane, not the ramp
10 show often one vehicle may change its mind
38 Mdecisions seen per policy in the DRL shot, 500 updates
3.6 hwall time per policy in the shot, 7 at once

Why it is called deep and reinforcement

Deep: the policy is a neural network, here small, 2 layers of 64. Reinforcement: nobody shows it correct answers. It only gets a score after acting, so it must try things and learn from the score.

Where the hope for an edge comes from

A fixed rule gives the same headway whatever is happening. The policy sees speed, gaps and position, so it can react. That is worth something only where the best headway changes with conditions it can see. Sections 12 and 13 show where that holds on this plant.

What it cannot do

It cannot brake, steer, change lane or hold the ramp. It cannot act when the vehicle ahead is not an ALKS. It knows nothing about the future and has no road model. Section 4 shows how much of the time its action has any effect.

All pictures with real numbers below come from one trace, for teaching. Stored policy C1 from the DRL shot (docs/research/phase3/shot_policies/C1_final.pt), trained on the earlier plant P0, driven on plant_c3 at 5,300 veh/h on used seed 7,419,640, once steady (S) and once with slowdown X1, 1,500 s each. It is not a result: one policy, one seed, not the plant it was trained on. Results are the V rows, which link to the main page. The training curves in section 11 are from the 7 shot policies on P0.

2. Five clocks

In one line. Everything runs on five clocks. Most confusion about this project's plant and reward comes from which clock a thing is on, as V367 showed.

Why this matters. The reward reads braking only on the whole-second ticks. Between two ticks there are 10 simulation steps, and a short hard braking can start and end inside them. That is how P0 hid 9 m/s² braking from every 1-Hz count (V367). The fix made the plant itself gentler; it did not make the reward faster.

One update is 3 episodes side by side, one each at 4,090, 4,600 and 5,300 veh/h. Episodes hold many vehicles, so an update holds tens of thousands of decisions even though one vehicle decides only about 30-70 times in its trip. Measured on the shot, C*_updates.jsonl: decisions per update 69,000-88,000.

3. What it sees

In one line. The policy gets 16 numbers about one vehicle, each divided by a hand-picked constant and most clipped to -1...1. It sees nothing else: no time, no demand, no map, no warning of a slowdown. Measured below: they are scaled by hand, not normalised, and one of them is dead.

It sees present states only

No time, demand or memory. Two identical situations get the same answer whether the slowdown has lasted 10 s or 100 s. It can only infer a slowdown through low speed in its own bin or the merge zone.

Merge 2 has less coverage

Input [13] covers merge 1 only: in the code, roads 3a and the ends of 2 and 3 are the merge zone, while 4a, 4 and 5 are all "downstream". Merge 2 reaches the policy only through x, [12], [14] and [15].

[7] tells it when acting is pointless

When the leader is not an ALKS the action has no effect, and [7] is 0. The policy can see this, but it still gets a decision, and that decision can matter later, because the target carries over.

MeasuredAll 69,360 decisions of the trace, at 5,300 veh/h; the other demand levels would differ a little. Normalised inputs would have mean near 0 and spread near 1. These do not: most are 0-to-1 ratios with spreads of 0.1 to 0.3. The code has no running mean-and-spread layer (c_train.py).

Dead input: [11] hold left

A vehicle is asked only when its own 10-s clock is due, and it can move only once per 10 s, so the wait left is always 0 when it is asked. That has been so since per-vehicle decisions came in (V290). Proof: its 64 weights moved exactly 0 in 500 updates, because a zero input gets a zero gradient. So the policy really has 15 inputs. Harmless: 0 × weight adds nothing to any decision.

Saturated: [1] and [14]

x/300 sits at -1 or +1 in 93 % of decisions, and nearest accel-lane vehicle in 84 %. Clipping is deliberate, since they matter only when near, but [1] centres on merge 1 only. Merge 2 has only the coarse x/1000 for its position, plus [14] and [15].

Does it hurt?

Not measured. A tanh network can compensate through its weights, and it seems to: [15], with a small spread, moved its weights most (RMS 0.32), and [0], with the largest spread, among the least (0.06). A suggestion from 16 points, not a test. Normalising observations is often advised for PPO: Andrychowicz et al., 2021, What Matters for On-Policy Deep Actor-Critic Methods? [VERIFY, from memory]. Whether it would help here is unknown.

What changed for confirmatory 3 (revision 4, V388-V390). Training now scales actor and critic inputs by a running mean and SD, updated only between updates, clipped at 5, and saved with the weights. The dead input [11] is set to 0, and [14] no longer counts the vehicle itself. Everything else on this page, including the live network in section 6 and the traces, comes from policy C1, trained before that with the inputs in this table.

The critic sees 10 more numbers

The critic is only for training, so it may use road-wide values that a vehicle would not have. It gets the same 16 plus these 10. That is the "centralised training, decentralised execution" idea: section 10.

Scaled the same way, and some less well: in this trace merge-zone count has a spread of 0.03 and insertion queue never passes 0.06 of its range. The critic's error matters less for use, since it is discarded after training.

4. What it does

In one line. The policy names a target among 4 headways. Between that wish and the car's behaviour lie four filters, and the last is traffic itself.

Code: _apply at v5b/fleet/b_env.py:652, _v2v at :730, want = min(want, v2v_cur + rise) at :744.

5. What it is paid

In one line. The reward is the only thing that tells the policy what we want. It is paid per vehicle per second, and it has parts each vehicle controls and parts nobody controls alone.

Try it: reward calculator

The term that teaches 0.8 s

1.6 s1.2 s1.0 s0.8 s
SteadySlowdown X1

Read the left chart. Following at 0.8 s rather than 1.6 s earns about +0.24 per second at motorway speed, and the vehicle gets it directly, from its own action. Nothing else in the reward responds so directly to the headway. So the policy learns to prefer 0.8 s almost everywhere, which is what V339 found: the policies rediscover 0.8 s.

MeasuredRead the right chart. When steady, own and near speed cost about what the flow term pays. Safety averages -0.11, about as large, although only 0.24 % of seconds carry a TTC flag and 0.45 % a hard-braking flag: at -10, one flagged second cancels about 17 seconds of the maximum flow term.

What the reward does not contain

No fuel, no comfort, no jerk, no door-to-door delay of the vehicle itself, no queue on the ramp except through the shared count. A metric outside the reward can only improve by accident. The protocol reports delay and fuel anyway.

Credit: who earned what

33 % of the reward's mean magnitude is shared when steady, 43 % in X1 (trace), and one vehicle among 200-300 barely moves it. Before the per-vehicle terms worked, every vehicle got the same score (V294), so a good action and a bad one looked alike. Section 10.

The reward and the winning metric overlap

TTC below 3 s is in the reward and is also the metric on which confirmatory 2 was won. Rules are not trained on it. It is a surrogate, and V377 found it mostly marks a slow queue around merge 2, with a median follower speed of 5-7 m/s. So the protocol gates the word "safety".

A real bug, kept as a lesson (V294). A rewrite dropped the call that computed the per-vehicle terms. It only showed in training, where report_net is off. Every check ran with it on, so all checks passed while all per-CAV runs trained on the shared term alone, and explanations were written for behaviour that had this cause. Now the training path calls _net_stats_gap, and smoke tests run in training mode. With the intended reward, the policies then learned fast and consistently in the first 84 updates (V295).

6. The networks

In one line. Each network is a stack of very simple units called neurons. Each neuron multiplies its inputs by its weights, adds them up, and squeezes the result. Training only changes those weights. The tool below runs the real weights of stored policy C1 in your browser, so what you see is the policy's real calculation.

The numbers in this sketch only illustrate the idea; the tool has the real ones. Code: _mlp and Net, v5b/fleet/c_train.py:34-48. Count for the actor: (16×64+64) + (64×64+64) + (64×4+4) = 1,088 + 4,160 + 260 = 5,508. No layer is shared between actor and critic.

What training did to the numbers

Inputs to layer 1Layer 1 to layer 2Layer 2 to scores
Inputs to layer 1Layer 1 to layer 2Layer 2 to scores
Free road, ALKS ahead: p(0.8 s)In the X1 queue: p(1.6 s)Unsure: p(0.8 s)

MeasuredStored policy C1 at each saved checkpoint; update 0 is rebuilt from the training seed. The weights keep moving through update 500 while the reward in section 11 has long been flat. Clear-cut states settle by about update 100. A state near a boundary does not: the third one, chosen because it is undecided at the end, fell from p = 0.93 at update 300 to 0.21 at update 500. So a flat reward does not mean a fixed policy, and a checkpoint chosen a little earlier could act differently in such states.

From scores to one choice

The 4 scores are called logits. Only their differences matter. Softmax turns them into probabilities: raise e to each score, divide by the total. Entropy measures how undecided the result is: 1.386 for 4 equal choices, 0 for a certain one. e^entropy reads as "how many choices it is really considering".

Try it: from 4 scores to a choice

Training: stochastic

Each decision is drawn at random from the probabilities (_act, c_train.py:94). The vehicle therefore tries other levels, and the critic and advantage can judge them. This is the exploration.

Use: greedy

Each decision takes the largest probability (Greedy, c_train.py:51). All evaluation runs are greedy, so behaviour in evaluation differs from behaviour in training. That is one reason the training reward does not predict the evaluation result.

Why so small

My reading: small networks train faster and are less able to memorise the training seeds. This one is about 11,000 numbers in total. Whether a larger one would find more was not the question of confirmatory 3: its budget and architecture were fixed before data.

7. Value and advantage

In one line. Reward says how the last second went. The policy needs to know how a choice went, and its effects arrive later. The critic bridges that gap by predicting the future reward of a state.

Value: V(state) = the critic's guess of r(now) + γ r(next) + γ² r(next+1) + ... Surprise: δ(t) = r(t) + γ V(t+1) - V(t), better or worse than expected, one step Advantage: A(t) = δ(t) + γλ δ(t+1) + (γλ)² δ(t+2) + ..., surprises blended over later steps (GAE) Return target: G(t) = A(t) + V(t), what the critic is trained to predict

Code: gae, v5b/fleet/c_train.py:69. It runs backward through a vehicle's trip: last = r[t] + gamma*next_v - v[t] + gamma*lam*last. One step is one 10-s decision, and r is that interval's mean reward per second, so a steady reward r gives V = r / (1-γ), about 15 times r at γ 0.933.

Try it: how far ahead does the policy look?

Both settings in the buttons look about 150 s ahead, which is roughly the time to cross a merge area and feel the result: V309 corrected an earlier, wrong reading of 25 s. My reasoning, not measured: too short and a vehicle cannot connect a gap it opens now with a merge that goes smoothly a minute later. Too long and the estimate is mostly noise, because 200 other vehicles decide what happens in between.

Why λ exists

λ near 0 trusts the critic after one step: low noise, but biased if the critic is wrong. λ near 1 uses the real rewards all the way: unbiased, but noisy. 0.967 per 10 s here is close to the 0.9 per 30 s of the code's default, c_train.py:29.

Why the critic uses a fixed scale

Returns are divided by a scale fixed once at update 0, so the critic predicts numbers near 1. It comes from the first batch and differed from 1.39 to 3.40 across the 7 shot learners. Section 11 shows what that does to the value-loss curve.

What happens when a vehicle leaves

A vehicle that leaves the road or reaches the episode's end is cut, not ended: the critic's value stands in for what would follow (c_train.py:144, :158). So leaving the network is not treated as the end of the reward.

8. State, action, reward

In one line. State is what the vehicle may use, action is what it may change, reward is the price list. Everything else exists to turn those three into one number to raise: the objective J, the mean discounted reward. Below, all of it runs on one real trip.

Try it: the loop on one real vehicle

From this decision to the objective

Each bar is one later decision's real reward × γ^k. Move γ and see how far ahead counts. The code's target also blends in the critic, by λ; that is the "target used". Real training does this on all vehicles, with γ 0.933 and λ 0.967.

The same trip, in detail

Things to look for, steady

The target mostly sits at 0.8 s in free flow. It falls toward 1.6 s around merge 2. Level follows target one step at a time, so it lags. Reward drops sharply at the merge areas: a single flagged second costs -10, which is -1 over a 10-s mean.

Things to look for, X1

The vehicle crawls for a long time in the queue, and the target sits at or near 1.6 s. Reward and advantage stay strongly negative. My reading: this critic was trained on another plant and with one random slowdown per episode, so here it expects better than happens. Negative advantage all along then shows a critic that is too optimistic, not a bad decision.

Why one action is hard to judge

A vehicle's level bites only with the gate open. Its reward depends mostly on what 200 others and the road do. Its effects spread over the next minutes. PPO copes by averaging over about 76,000 decisions per update, and that is what makes one action's contribution visible at all.

How state, action and reward relate, measured

These are measured across all decisions of the trace. Click a row of the grid to see that input's curves. Hover for values. Blue means they rise together, orange means one rises as the other falls.

Reward lab: the prices decide what is best

Five behaviours ran on the same seed: the greedy policy, and everyone at one fixed level. The grid splits each one's score into its parts, per ALKS-second. Change the prices and watch the ranking: the objective is nothing but these prices × these events.

TrafficPrices

One seed, not a result. Differences here include chance: fixing a small side effect of an earlier trace script alone moved this policy's X1 flow by 33 vehicles (2,131 to 2,164). Repricing also keeps behaviour frozen; real training under new prices would change the policy, and the ranking with it. V339, V359 and V368 are the evidence on how policy and rules compare.

The objective is not the thesis metric

J is what training raises. Delay, flow, TTC and braking are what the protocol judges. They overlap only where a term of the reward touches a metric, so a better J does not by itself mean a better road.

9. One PPO update

In one line. PPO asks: given what just happened, how should the probabilities move, without moving them so far that the batch stops being a fair guide?

ratio = new probability of the action taken / old probability clip term = -mean(min(ratio × A, clamp(ratio, 1-ε, 1+ε) × A)), ε = 0.2 value term = mean((V(state) - return target/scale)²) loss = clip term + 0.5 × value term - 0.01 × entropy

Code: update, v5b/fleet/c_train.py:177. Why clipped: the batch was collected with the old policy, so it says little about a much different one. With positive A, there is no gain from pushing the ratio above 1+ε. With negative A, no gain from pushing it below 1-ε.

10. One brain, many cars

In one line. There are hundreds of agents but only one set of numbers. Each vehicle uses the same policy with its own inputs, and all their experience trains it. Textbook names: parameter sharing, and centralised training with decentralised execution.

Why share

A vehicle only lives about 30-70 decisions. With separate policies each would have almost no data and the policy would die with the vehicle. Sharing gives 38 million decisions to one set of numbers.

The price of sharing

Vehicles in the same situation act the same way, apart from their random draws. Greedy use removes the draws, so two neighbours with similar inputs pick the same level. It cannot assign one vehicle to open a gap and the next to close it, unless their inputs differ.

The credit problem

The shared terms are the same for all. If 250 vehicles act, each one's effect on them is about 1/250 and is buried in noise. That is why the reward has per-vehicle terms, including the follower's TTC and braking. Before those worked, learning was poor (V294).

A moving target

Each vehicle's surroundings are other vehicles run by the same policy, which changes every update. What was a good choice can stop being so. The clip and the fresh batch per update limit this but do not remove it.

Why a road-wide critic helps

The critic only predicts. Giving it road-wide state, such as the zone speeds and queue, lets it explain away what the vehicle could not control, which leaves a cleaner advantage for the actor. The actor stays deployable, because it needs only what a vehicle knows. This is my reading of the method; the effect on this plant was not measured.

Staggered decisions

Vehicles have their own 10-s clocks, aligned to the 5-s environment steps. So at each step about half of them are asked (due, b_env.py:880). V290 introduced this after a run with 5-s decisions and a 30-s limit gave near-uniform probabilities. Its explanation was withdrawn in V294, because the reward was broken at the time; the per-vehicle clock stayed.

11. Reading training

In one line. Four curves tell you if training is alive. They do not tell you if the result is good. These come from the DRL shot: 7 learners, 500 updates, r2m3 on the earlier plant P0, about 3.6 h each. Confirmatory 3 will produce the same files on plant_c3.

Grey: each learner. Blue: their mean. Points are means over 10 updates, except the first, which is update 0 alone. Hover for values. From revision 4, the logs also hold KL, clip fraction and explained variance per update, and a pilot file with the first input statistics (V388).

Reward: flat is not dead

It climbs from about -0.21 to -0.18 in the first 50-100 updates, then stays near -0.17 (V364). Noise per update is about 0.08, because each update draws new seeds and slowdowns. So reward here cannot prove learning after update 100, and it cannot compare runs on different plants: references, weights and vehicle counts all differ.

Entropy: the real sign of learning

From about 1.38, nearly uniform, to about 0.7 by update 150. e^0.7 is about 2, so the policy now hesitates between about 2 levels on average. Falling means it commits. A collapse to near 0 early would mean it stopped exploring, which did not happen.

Value loss: read with care

The logged curves look very different across learners, 0.15 to 0.83. Multiply by scale² and they match: about 1.6-1.9 by the end, down from about 2.6-3.3. So the difference was only units. The critic's typical error is about √1.7 ≈ 1.3, on values near -8 in the traced trips. Scale matters beyond units: the gradient limit applies to actor and critic together, so a larger value term can shrink the actor's step. Not measured.

What these curves cannot say

None of them measures how the policy does against a rule. That needs fresh seeds, greedy use and paired comparison. V297 to V298 is the warning: a policy met the bar at 5,300, then failed on fresh seeds.

Checks run before any of this was drawn

  • 5 learners × 500 updates, each update exactly once; no crashed first attempts.
  • Every episode's seed is its environment's next one in the approved training block; pilot seeds are separate and unused for learning.
  • Every update has exactly one 1,500-s episode at each demand level, 4,090, 4,600 and 5,300 veh/h.
  • Critic scale fixed after update 0; no missing or non-finite values in any update.
  • Network-wide counts are absent in training, as designed, and the merge-cap actuator never acted.
  • The checks were shown to fire first: 4 faults planted in a copy of the logs, all 4 caught, no false alarms.
  • TensorBoard: 119,995 values written and read back, 0 mismatches.
  • Independent recomputation from the raw logs, with its own slowdown draw: 30,210 values, 0 mismatches.

Not the result

None of these curves says whether the policies beat the rules. That is the evaluation on fresh seeds, read by the protocol's fixed rules. A smooth training curve has misled this project before (V297-V298).

Explained variance is flattering

It compares the critic with targets that contain the critic's own values (lambda-returns), so it overstates how well the critic predicts outcomes. Use its trend, not its level.

Merge 2 is not in the traffic counts

In training, TTC and braking are counted on merge 1's lanes only, once a second. Network counts are not measured in training; the check confirms they are absent, not zero.

TensorBoard smoothing

TensorBoard draws a smoothed line by default. Set the smoothing slider to 0 to see the raw values; this page shows 10-update means and says so.

12. What it learned

In one line. Trained, the policy is a map from situation to headway. Plot it and you can read it like a rule: a mostly fixed 0.8 s, with longer headways where traffic is slow.

Each cell is a 100-m by 2-m/s box. Stronger blue means shorter target. Stored policy C1, one seed, not a result. Cell mean over all decisions there, including those with a closed gate.

Along the road: policy against rules

Level 3 = 0.8 s, 0 = 1.6 s, per ALKS-second. Roads to scale, so 3a and 4a are narrow; hover for their values.

MeasuredThe policy holds nearly 0.8 s on most of the road when traffic flows, and drops on road 4a to level 1.6. In X1 the queue from road 4 pushes road 3 from level 2.5 down to 1.4, and road 4a to 1.0. So it reacts to the slowdown, seen through speed, with no knowledge of its time or place.

InferenceReading the map as a mechanism: the policy opens gaps where traffic is slow and merges are close. V361 and V368 name what this means in outcomes: fewer seconds at TTC below 3 s than p333, at similar delay. Whether the reacting part is what pays, or just the fixed position part, is what the copy rule tests in confirmatory 3: it uses the policy's mean level per road and nothing else.

13. DRL and the plant

In one line. A DRL result belongs to a plant. Each row is a plant fact, what it does to learning, and where it was found. If you change a row, old policies and old conclusions do not carry over.

Plant factWhat it isWhat it does to the DRLFound in
V2V gateAction works only behind an ALKS within 150 m with the same leader on two updatesAction bites about 51 % of ALKS-seconds. In the rest, a chosen level has no effect, so the reward signal for it is noiseV277, V286
50 % ALKSHalf the vehicles run their own model and ignore the policyHalf the possible leaders are not ALKS, so the gate closes often. Other shares are a different problem; V299 mapped 25 and 80 % on the earlier plantV299
tau as the actuatorSets the wanted gap, not the speedTau is a floor (section 4), so its value depends on traffic density. My reading: it can raise capacity and open gaps, but cannot speed up a stuck queueV282, V289
Own-spacing flow termPays for short spacing directlyStrongly teaches 0.8 s. A policy that sits at 0.8 s is the expected outcome, which ties p333 when conditions do not changeV339
Rate limitOne level per 10 sStops chatter. Also means up to 20 s to swing fully, and a shock that lasts seconds cannot be answeredV278, V290
Rise limit, plant_c3Longer tau grows at 0.2 s per second; shorter applies at onceRemoves hidden braking when a leader changes. Without it, part of DRL's edge could have been avoiding an artefact. Costs p333 10-13 % delay under slowdowns, 2 seedsV377, V378, V382
Plant fix P0 → P0dLowering a speed cap no longer brakes at 9 m/s²Policies trained on P0 trained on another plant. So confirmatory 3 retrains from scratch; stored policies are only for teachingV367, V376
1-Hz rewardBraking and TTC are read on the whole secondA short hard braking between samples costs nothing. Now rarer because the plant is gentler, but the reward's eye is the same. Protocol metrics check at step levelV367, V380
No-control referencesThe shared count term compares with a no-control run on that plant and demandChanging the plant changes the reward's zero. Rewards from two plants are not comparable. make_env.py checks the referencesV286, V376
Position bug, fix_xOn r2m3, x used nominal lengths and was clipped at 3.0 kmThe shot and earlier r2m3 policies saw slightly wrong positions at the far end. Fixed in plant_c3V378
Input scalingHand-picked constants until V387; running mean and SD from revision 4Spreads differed up to about 7 times, one input was dead and one read 0 for merging vehicles. Fixed before confirmatory 3's training; earlier policies keep the old inputsV387, V388, V389
Zone definitionThe merge zone holds merge 1 onlyMerge 2 reaches the policy through position and local inputs. Speculation: this may be part of why rule forms on 4a do wellV361
Random slowdowns2 of 3 training episodes: edge 3, 4 or 5, 25-60 km/h, 60-180 s, starting 400-1,200 sX2 lies inside this range. X1 uses its lowest speed and holds two events, where training holds one. So they test the trained range more than surprisesV358
TTC in reward and metricThe policy is paid for the metric on which it is judgedA win on TTC is partly expected, and rules were not tuned for that alone until revision 3 chose opponents by lowest TTC. TTC here marks slow queues around merge 2V377, V378
Steady versus slowdownWith steady demand the best headway barely changesNo hidden condition to adapt to, so a good fixed rule ties. Slowdowns give the policy a job. That is why they are the primary cellsV339, V359

The reward's eye and the plant's clock

V367 measured the real case on P0: 1,749 vehicle-seconds at 7 m/s² or harder, on one seed at 5,300, while the 1-Hz metric read 0. Plant_c3 removes the source; the moving full-emergency events are 0 in all arms in the pre-run checks (V382).

14. How we got here

In one line. Each attempt changed the action, the reward or the plant. So far no pre-registered run has shown a delay win over rules.

AttemptActionIdeaWhat happened
A: merge capOne central policy lowers a speed cap on ALKS near merge 1Slowing down is the only lever, so it learned to slowRun 1 no learning (V266). A fixed 30 km/h cap beat every policy on safety proxies (V267). Efficiency reward: still slows, flow unchanged (V272). Named the slowing bias (V271)
B: zone headwaysOne central policy, a target per zone, every 10 sHeadway instead of speed, so slowing is no longer the only wayNeeds a rate limit: up-down-up-down without one (V278). Trades flow for fewer short gaps (V279). Run 5 fails the bar (V285)
Per-CAVShared policy, target per ALKSLocal inputs, per-vehicle rewardCollapse toward 1.6 s (V288). Near-uniform at 5-s decisions (V290). Reward bug found, explanations of V288-V293 withdrawn (V294). Fixed: meets the bar at 5,300 only, fails fresh seeds (V297, V298). 0 of 10 cells against p303 (V300). No DRL setting passes on m32 (V304)
r1m3 P0Same, plus optional speed and lane actionsStart from an almost perfect plant, tune no control firstPolicies rediscover 0.8 s and tie the rule (V339). Speed-cap oracle shows no headroom, KILL for that action (V344)
r2m3Same, two merges, slowdownsGive the policy a job a fixed rule may miss1 of 20 cells won, on TTC, not delay (V359). r4a1 matched, then did not hold on fresh seeds (V361, V368). Review finds hidden braking (V367)
Confirmatory 3Same action; no speed actionFixed plant, retrained, 70 rules as opponents, closure ruleRunning since 09:20 today (V383). If no primary cell is won, this DRL line closes on these slowdowns (V378)
A pattern to remember. Three times a reading had to be corrected because something else caused what was seen: a count that measured stopped queues, not risky following (V283), a dropped reward term (V294), and a plant that hid braking (V367). A surprising DRL result should first be traced as a possible plant or code cause.

15. How it will be judged

In one line. 5 fresh policies, tuned rules chosen on separate seeds, fixed margins, and a sentence for each outcome, all written before the data.

ReadingA primary cell (X1 or X2 at 5,300) is won if at least 4 of 5 policies...Role
Tuned, on TTCagainst every opponent that counts: TTC at least 10 % better, CI excluding 0, at least 20 per run lower; delay at most 2 % worse; flow at most 0.5 % worse; braking at 3 m/s² at most 5 % worseDecides the claim
Delay winagainst the lower-delay of the delay opponent and p333: delay at least 5 % better, CI excluding 0; flow at most 0.5 % worse; TTC and braking at most 10 % worseAlso counts as won
Replicationagainst p333: TTC at least 30 % better, with this protocol's limits and countersReported; does earlier V359 survive the plant fix?

Shortened here. The full text and the extra limits are in docs/research/protocols/confirmatory_3.md, sections Claim rules and Sentences allowed. Revision 4 (V390) changed only the policy inputs, before any policy data. The word "safety" needs one more check on samples at 3 m/s² or harder. Otherwise the sentence says "fewer seconds at TTC below 3 s".

What to look at first when it ends

1. decide3_table.csv: did at least 4 of 5 clear? 2. Which opponents counted, and did only p333 count? 3. The copy rule: if it matches the policies, the reacting part adds nothing. 4. Map cells: where are policies clearly worse?

Three ways to read the outcome

Won on TTC: an advantage of reacting, on a surrogate, on an uncalibrated plant. Replication only: the old edge held against 0.8 s, not against tuned rules. Neither: the edge did not survive the fixed plant, and the line closes.

Why a loss is still a result

A pre-registered negative on the fixed plant, with tuned opponents and a logged path, is usable thesis material. V368's edge could still have been real on P0 and yet belong to what P0 hid.

16. Glossary, self-check

Glossary

WordMeans here
Actor / policyNetwork from inputs to action probabilities. The thing kept after training.
Critic / value functionNetwork that predicts future reward from a state. Thrown away after training.
AdvantageWhat happened minus what the critic expected. Sign tells the actor which way to move.
Discount γHow much the next decision's reward counts. 0.933 per 10 s here.
GAE λHow much later surprises count when computing the advantage.
EntropyHow undecided the probabilities are. 1.386 is uniform among 4.
EpisodeOne SUMO run of 1,500 s.
UpdateOne round: collect 3 episodes, then 10 passes of gradient steps.
GreedyTake the most likely action. Used in all evaluations.
Parameter sharingOne set of numbers for all vehicles.
BootstrappingUsing the critic's value in place of rewards not yet seen.
LevelIndex of the target: 0 = 1.6 s, 1 = 1.2 s, 2 = 1.0 s, 3 = 0.8 s.
Gate (V2V)The condition under which a target applies at all.
p333The fixed rule: 0.8 s in all zones.
r4a1A fixed rule: 1.2 s on road 4a, 0.8 s elsewhere.
plant_c3P0d plus tau_rise 0.2, taper_fast and fix_x, on r2m3.

Check yourself

Why does the policy mostly choose 0.8 s, even though nothing tells it to?

The flow term pays each vehicle for short spacing, directly from its own action. At motorway speed, following at 0.8 s rather than 1.6 s earns about +0.24 per second. Nothing else responds so directly. It holds 0.8 s until a stronger term, such as the -10 TTC or braking flags, pushes back.

A policy picks level 3 while its leader is a human car. What happens?

The target is remembered, and the level may still move, but the gate is closed, so tau stays 1.6 s. Once it has the same ALKS leader on two updates, tau falls to the level's value at once.

Reward stays flat from update 100 to 500. Has it stopped learning?

Not necessarily. Entropy still falls a little, moves and reversals drop, and the reward's noise (about 0.08 per update) can hide small gains. But it also shows no large gain is coming. Only evaluation can say how good it is.

Why can't you compare a reward from P0 and a reward from plant_c3?

The shared count term is relative to a no-control run on that plant, and other terms change with the plant's traffic. The same number means different things.

Why does X1 show strongly negative advantages for a trip that looks sensible?

This stored critic was trained on P0, not plant_c3, and it expects better than happens there. Advantage measures against the critic, so a wrong critic gives a wrong sign of surprise. In training the critic would adapt; here it is frozen.

If the copy rule matches the policies, what have you learned?

That the policies' value is in where they use which headway, which a fixed table can reproduce. The reacting part, using speed in real time, would not be adding anything measurable on those cells.

What is one weight, in plain words?

One number that says how much one neuron's output pushes one neuron in the next layer, up if positive and down if negative. Nothing else in the policy is learned. Training is only 5,508 of these being moved a little, many times.

In the reward lab, the policy scores best at the trained prices. Does that mean it is better?

It means it earned more of what it was trained to earn, on one seed. That is close to automatic. The protocol asks a different question: does it beat tuned rules on delay, flow and TTC, on fresh seeds, across policies.

Why are 5 policies needed, and why at least 4 of 5?

One policy can win by luck of its random start. Requiring most of them to clear the bar tests the method and not one draw. No checkpoint or policy is selected.

What would change if the reward were sampled every 0.1 s?

Short hard brakings would cost what they should. It would be 10 times as many reward reads, and P0's hidden braking would probably have been paid for. It was not tested.

Limits of this page

Teaching trace: one stored policy trained on P0, one used seed, 2 conditions, driven on plant_c3 where it was not trained. All policy maps, composition charts and trips are illustrations, not results. Training curves: the shot, on P0. Formula charts assume exact steady following. "My reading" marks explanations not separately tested. Numbers from V rows link to the main page, where the sources are named. The live network runs the stored weights rounded to 4 decimals; a check at build time compares it with PyTorch. The learning step in section 6 is one plain gradient step on one decision, made large enough to see; real training uses Adam, 4,096 decisions at a time and a smaller step. Sources beside this page: drl_trace.py and drl_trace2.py, run from the repo root at fae4620, with outputs drl_trace_S.json, drl_trace_X1.json and drl_lab.json. The page builder is in /home/catalin/work/phd/v5b1_runs/phase3/scratch/extract/, outside git. After confirmatory 3 ends, this page can be rebuilt from its policies.
